quote: The correct answer is not available to you as a hypothesis, because it will not be invented for another thirty years.
content: A realist, single-world, deterministic account was available from the beginning. De Broglie presented the pilot-wave theory at the 1927 Solvay conference, before the Copenhagen orthodoxy had formed; it was criticized by Pauli, set aside, and rediscovered and completed by Bohm in 1952 (Bohm (1952)), five years before Everett. It answers every question the essay puts to “Goofus”: the wavefunction is real, the particle has a definite position at all times, measurement is an ordinary interaction, and the Born statistics follow from an equilibrium distribution of initial positions. Bell, whose theorem the essay invokes, regarded pilot-wave theory as the demonstration that the “impossibility” of a realist account was a prejudice, and asked in print why it was ignored in the textbooks (Bell (1982)). The essay’s narrative, in which physicists who declined to be realists were making the best of a situation with no realist option, and in which the option arrived only with Everett, erases the one that existed for the entire period. The historical record of how the field treated it (Cushing, Quantum Mechanics: Historical Contingency and the Copenhagen Hegemony, 1994, a book with no DOI) is also the best available test of the next essay’s counterfactual about what happens to a realist theory that comes first.

quote: What does Goofus even mean, here? Never mind the plausibility of his words; what sort of state of reality would correspond to his words being true?
content: The question has been answered by the people who hold the view, and their answer is this book’s own epistemology applied to the quantum state. QBism (Fuchs, Mermin & Schack (2014)) holds that a quantum state is an agent’s credence, that the Born rule is a normative constraint on credences like the rules of probability, and that “collapse” is Bayesian updating; its founders cite Jaynes, whose Mind Projection Fallacy this book adopted in Probability Is in the Mind as the reason there is “no real probability.” Rovelli’s relational interpretation (Rovelli (1996)) makes the state a relation between systems, with a definite physical content. Both say what state of reality corresponds to their words: a world of systems and agents in which the wavefunction is not among the furniture, and in which the question “what determines my experimental results?” has the answer “the systems I interact with,” not “the amplitudes.” One may reject these views. But a book that spends six essays arguing that probability is a state of partial information and not a property of the world cannot then treat, as a semantic stop-sign, the position that the quantum state is a state of partial information and not a property of the world. That position is the book’s, taken one step further by physicists who read the same Jaynes.

quote: But Bell’s Theorem makes it much less plausible that the quantum equations are partial knowledge of something deterministic, the way that statistical mechanics over classical physics is partial knowledge of something deterministic.
content: The word that makes this sentence true is “local,” and it is omitted. Bell’s theorem rules out local hidden variables; the non-local deterministic completion, pilot-wave theory, survives it and was the theory Bell had in mind, since the theorem was written to find out whether Bohm’s nonlocality was avoidable (Bell, “On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen Paradox,” Bell (1964)). The “much less plausible” is an assessment of nonlocality, and the sequence treats nonlocality as disqualifying. But the theorem’s assumptions include that measurements have single outcomes, which is why Everett escapes it, and the claim that Everett is thereby “local” is itself debated (Wallace and Timpson for; Maudlin against, in the same 2010 volume). The choice the theorem leaves is between nonlocality and the denial of definite outcomes. The essay presents one horn as a “Get Out of Jail Free card” and the other as obvious; the theorem does not rank them, and the physicist who proved it took the first.
